title: All Circuits Lead to Rome: Non-Unique Mechanisms in LLMs
one_liner: A single task in a language model can be solved by multiple different internal circuits, each equally good but built completely differently.
lead: When you poke inside a language model to find how it does something—like recognizing a person's name—researchers have always assumed there is one main pathway, one set of neurons doing the work. This paper shows that is wrong. Multiple completely different pathways can do the same job, all at once, each one working perfectly and barely overlapping with the others. This changes how we should think about what the model is actually doing inside.

problem.h2: The search for how models work
paras: When a language model answers a question, billions of tiny numbers change state inside it. Researchers want to understand the real gears: which neurons fire, in what order, to produce the output. This is called circuit discovery—like tracing the path of electricity through a computer.

The unstated assumption was always: each task has ONE true circuit, maybe with a bit of noise. If you remove neurons not in that circuit, the model should fail. If you find the circuit, you have found THE mechanism. A beginner would assume a model either has the circuit or does not, the same way a radio either has a working path or a broken one.

callout.html: The model can do the same task multiple ways simultaneously, using completely different circuits that barely touch each other.

panels.title: 1. The old assumption
panels.caption: People thought: one task, one true circuit, one mechanism.

panels.title: 2. But in reality
panels.caption: Multiple different paths are active and strong, solving the same job.

panels.title: 3. They barely overlap
panels.caption: Each path uses different neurons; there is almost no sharing between them.

panels.title: 4. The paper's tool: penalize overlap
panels.caption: Force the discovery algorithm to find new circuits by pushing them apart.

panels.title: 5. Result: many circuits, same task
panels.caption: Each circuit works alone; none is the one true way.

steps.text: Use standard circuit discovery to extract neurons solving a task.
Count how many neurons are shared with circuits found before.
Add a cost to the discovery algorithm for each neuron used twice.
Run discovery again, pushing it toward a new set of neurons.
Check if each circuit works alone and all are sparse and distinct.

object.h2: The single thing this paper changes
paras: Instead of running circuit discovery once and trusting the result as THE mechanism, run it many times with an extra penalty that pushes each run to use different neurons. The penalty is applied during discovery—it steers the algorithm away from neurons already found in previous runs.

hidden.name: Shared neuron count
paras: When you discover a second circuit, some of its neurons might already be in the first circuit. That shared count is the overlap. A small overlap means the two circuits are structurally different; a large overlap means they are nearly the same path with minor tweaks.

The paper measures overlap as the fraction of neurons appearing in multiple discovered circuits. By penalizing this quantity during discovery, it forces each new circuit to use neurons avoided by the previous ones. The penalty grows stronger as overlap increases, steering the algorithm toward virgin territory—because a candidate circuit that reuses many neurons gets a lower score, and the algorithm only accepts circuits with high scores, so it must find new neurons to win.

heat.caption: Darker means more neurons; highlights show the paper's focus: unique circuits with minimal overlap.

reads.html: If two circuits use completely different neurons, they are structurally distinct even if both solve the task.
Overlap is measured as a Jaccard similarity or intersection cardinality between discovered neuron sets; the penalty term subtracts from the discovery objective proportionally.

mechanism.h2: Why many circuits can solve one task
paras: Inside a language model, there is enormous redundancy. Each neuron does not do one specific thing. Instead, information is distributed across thousands of neurons, all talking at once, with multiple concepts overlaid on the same neurons. One neuron might be part of a hundred different concepts.

Because of this redundancy, the same task can be wired many ways. Imagine a filing cabinet with ten billion slots, each holding a tiny number. You need to compute the answer to one question. There is no one way to do it: you could use slots 1–100, or slots 200–300, or even slots 7, 42, and 5001—all give the same answer. The model is so redundant and so high-dimensional that many non-overlapping solutions exist simultaneously.

The paper's method makes this visible by refusing to find the same solution twice. Each time you ask the algorithm to find a circuit, it must find a NEW one, in a different part of the model. By collecting several runs, you see that the model really does support multiple competing pathways, all solving the same task, all sparse and functional, all barely touching.

stages.s: A task: recognize names in text
Run circuit discovery with no overlap penalty
Run discovery again, penalizing overlap with the first circuit
Test if the new circuit still works alone
Multiple independent, non-overlapping circuits all solving the task

math.h2: The formula for discovering with repulsion
math.words: Score of a circuit equals (how well it performs the task) minus (how many neurons it shares with previously discovered circuits times a penalty strength).
symbols: How good this circuit is; higher is better
How well the circuit solves the task, ranging from 0 to 100 percent
Number of neurons appearing in this circuit and any previous one
The penalty strength; higher values push circuits further apart

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Circuit A: uses neurons 1, 5, 12, 23. Accuracy 95 percent.
Circuit B candidate: uses neurons 1, 5, 40, 41. Accuracy 92 percent. Overlap with A: 2 neurons (1 and 5).
Circuit C candidate: uses neurons 50, 60, 70, 80. Accuracy 91 percent. Overlap with A: 0.
Even though C is slightly less accurate, it scores higher because it is completely new. The algorithm picks C.

math.note: The penalty term steers discovery toward neurons unused before, forcing the algorithm to find completely different solutions to the same problem.

bars.h2: Comparing traditional discovery to overlap-aware discovery

charts.title: Traditional circuit discovery
charts.note: One run, one circuit. No knowledge of alternatives.

charts.title: Overlap-aware repulsion (this paper)
charts.note: Multiple runs, each finds a different path. All work, little sharing.

items.b: Circuits may degrade with strong penalties.
items.html: If lambda is too high, the algorithm sacrifices accuracy to find truly separate neurons. The discovered circuits still work but fail more easily when the input changes slightly.

items.b: Overlap measurements depend on the discovery method.
items.html: Different circuit discovery algorithms (like different sheaf methods) may find different neurons for the same mechanism. The overlap penalty is sensitive to which algorithm you use.
If circuits are ultra-sparse (only a few neurons), the problem looks more severe than it is. A slightly looser circuit might overlap more but reveal truer shared structure.
Use a moderate penalty, measure overlap consistently, and validate that each discovered circuit works independently before claiming success.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Pick a simple LLM task like detecting if a sentence contains a specific word. Use standard circuit discovery to find neurons solving it, recording the accuracy. Penalize overlap by a small amount and run discovery again, recording the new neurons and accuracy. Repeat five times. Plot each circuit's accuracy and the overlap between each pair. The demo should show that accuracy stays high while overlap stays low across runs.
demo.metric_eq: average_overlap = sum of (neurons_shared_i,j / total_neurons_in_circuit) for all pairs (i,j)
demo.closing: If multiple completely different circuits all solve the task with high accuracy, the false assumption of unique mechanisms is broken.
